title: Treasury Secretary crystalises Budget 2027  as Govt., vows consensus with private sector | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 04:57
-     - 71

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma

By Charumini de Silva

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma speaking at the 16th post-Budget Forum organised by the Daily FT and the University of Colombo MBA Alumni Association last Friday, said the Government would dedicate itself to implementing Budget 2027, while building consensus with the private sector, though any adjustments would have to be progressive and in the best interests of Sri Lanka.

The forum brought together experts and private sector leaders to discuss investment constraints under the IMF program, land ownership rules for foreigners, State-owned enterprise (SOE) reforms, tax compliance, and SME financing. 

Responding to private sector initial observations, Dr. Suriyapperuma said Budget 2027 was a continuation of a journey already begun and that the IMF program places certain limits on the support the Government can extend. 

“Certain provisions have been made, based on what we could afford and on the requests from the Chamber of Commerce and other stakeholders. But I agree that we need to support this segment more, so that we can attract more investment. To that end, the focus is policy certainty and credibility in how we engage. Whatever we can do is already in the facilitation process; bringing in new laws, reducing the time needed for approvals, and so on,” he explained.

On land ownership restrictions for foreigners, Dr. Suriyapperuma noted that Sri Lanka is a 65,000 square kilometre island nation and that certain areas require careful consideration. However, foreign companies can already acquire lands through listed entities, many of which have significant foreign shareholding.

“On the $ 3 million investment limit, the value is not the only criterion. Job creation and the location where a facility is to be established, reinvested in or expanded are also considered,” he said.

Acknowledging concerns about why the State remains in businesses such as hotels and fertiliser, he said the reforms should have been undertaken decades ago, but were not. “This administration has the opportunity to do it, and the Government's view is the same. Some 33 SOEs have been earmarked for closure. Of these 14 are at the final stage of closing down, while another 14 have been or will shortly be advertised through the Registrar of Companies (RoC), inviting objections from creditors or unidentified parties,” he said, adding where needed the Government will also consider exit options.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said the era in which the State had to make large investments is fast ending, but it will continue to invest where businesses are unwilling to take the first step or the risk, or where the investment is too large exiting on an appropriate basis. “This is why committees have been appointed to re-examine these engagements. So, whether it is hotels, fertiliser or anything else, the question is which areas are absolutely necessary for the Government to stay in and play a role,” he added.

Regarding the fertiliser voucher scheme, the Treasury Secretary said it will not be replaced. Farmers would be free to choose where to buy, as the voucher carries a value that can be redeemed at the best competitive offer. He cited the education sector, where students receive a Rs. 6,000 digital voucher with a QR code, instead of books from an SOE and could redeem it from the bookstore offering the best deal. “Fertiliser voucher is the same digital mechanism. It is meant to encourage competition and to benefit businesses and citizens,” Dr. Suriyapperuma said.

Participants and the panellists also put a range of contentious questions to the Treasury Secretary.

Below are excerpts of the audience Q&A;

People are now required to have it if they are transferring land, buying vehicles and so on. This is a process, and I'm sure society will embrace these requirements. It will reduce the gap between the compliant and the non-compliant, which gives compliant taxpayers the advantage they are seeking

Q: Under the Budget, some items are being removed fully and 697 items are being cut by 50% on the Cess. What exact criteria are used to protect local manufacturers who depend on the domestic supply chain from being undercut by cheaper importers? Some items have already been 100% removed. What are the exact criteria?

A: Thank you. This is a four-year journey. Some items are already removed and others will go in 2027, 2028 and 2029. That is why we have taken steps to make sure local manufacturers are looked after in the process, for example by introducing product standards. At present, products without any standards can be brought into Sri Lanka and sold at much lower prices, because they are made without complying with environmental and labour requirements that are accepted in today's world. Standards are being brought in so that local industry can compete, provided local industry also meets those requirements and upgrades. We want industries to prosper by producing high-quality products at competitive rates, with the technologies the world is asking for.

That is also why the Government is providing financing support. Industries affected by the removal of para-tariffs may need additional support to invest in upgrading their standards, quality and laboratories. Last year Rs. 100 million was given to the SLSI and other institutions to upgrade their testing equipment. We have also moved away from the requirement that only Sri Lankan tests are accepted; Sri Lanka now accepts accredited laboratory certificates from other countries, which creates a level playing field.

Standards are not only an advantage to local companies. International and local producers compete at the same level, and consumers get the best choice. In the transition, there is a lot of financing support to upgrade skills, manufacturing facilities and testing facilities. That is why a four-year period is used instead of one year. If everything were removed in a single year, things would be different. This is a transition and a facilitation. We know how much employment depends on these industries, so the Government is conscious of it and will implement it carefully over time. 

Q: Compliant businesses lament they can’t compete with non-compliant rivals, especially on VAT, and are going out of business. Compliance is penalised while evasion pays. On income tax, absurd assessments are common. Appeals go back to the IRD, which seldom overturns its own decisions, before moving to higher appeals. Can compliance, especially on VAT, be improved? And could a taxpayer rights ombudsman or a more independent appeal process be introduced? The current system discourages genuine taxpayers.

A: I suppose that has been the culture in this country. It is a change of that culture over time. To build a compliant culture, TIN was mandated. People are now required to have it if they are transferring land, buying vehicles and so on. This is a process, and I'm sure society will embrace these requirements. It will reduce the gap between the compliant and the non-compliant, which gives compliant taxpayers the advantage they are seeking.

On appeals, there are multiple layers. The first is the IRD officials themselves, who have the flexibility to reverse or change a decision, which is much faster than another process. Second, there is the Tax Appeals Commission, chaired by retired Judges, who understand the justice system as well as the taxpayer's point of view. And if the taxpayer is still not happy, the judicial system is available. Our view is also to simplify these processes and bring efficiency to them. It takes time, because the country is used to doing things differently. 

Q: Budget proposal implementation is a key challenge. With 73 proposals and about Rs. 400 billion for next year, monitoring is critical. I saw no real Budget monitoring in Parliament last year. Asking as a citizen, because 2027 is pivotal. Will you commit to at least five monitoring categories; financial, physical project, economic impact, social impact, and transparency and accountability? If Rs. 200 billion isn't utilised by April 2027, the country is in trouble, the Government will collapse and the country will collapse. 

A: I suppose everyone agrees, and as a nation we did not do this for many decades, and many are responsible for ignoring those responsibilities. The country came to this position not by choice. It was deliberate as a result of poor policies, bad policies and unwise investment decisions. There were multiple reasons for the collapse, not only a lack of monitoring.

On monitoring, there are multiple mechanisms built into the system. One example is how we monitored the Rs. 97 billion of finance going to the SME sector; regular interventions and interactions with that segment, and quarterly reports to Cabinet on progress. There is a dedicated project monitoring department for projects above Rs. 1 billion, and last year we lowered the threshold so that projects above Rs. 250 million are monitored. If there are implementation challenges, they can be escalated to decision-makers. So the point is taken. It is very important, and the Government is actively engaged.

But the speculation that there will be challenges in the near future is completely unfounded. I think the President addressed that concern during his Budget speech. In 2025 alone, the amount we paid in foreign-currency debt servicing was more than the amount we are due to pay in 2028. It is a popular tagline for many reasons, but we should recognise that it is unfounded, and also that there are many areas where we can improve implementation.

For example, in 2025 Sri Lanka achieved nearly 80% capital expenditure implementation (78%+). The Budget was approved late, so funds were available only from around April onwards, which left about nine months. A month of that was lost to Cyclone Ditwah, so we had about eight months to deliver, and in that time the Government delivered nearly 80% of the allocation. That shows that capacity and monitoring ability are improving.

To implement these projects, we also need the private sector's support and capacity. A particular challenge this year was the Middle East war. The supplies were not available, for road projects for instance, and prices escalated sharply. Some contractors found it cheaper to let their performance bonds be forfeited than to execute the contract. The Government intervened, revised the procurement guidelines and gave the necessary support for them to continue. We will keep reacting and monitoring these situations closely. Thank you for the suggestion.

Standards are not only an advantage to local companies. International and local producers compete at the same level, and consumers get the best choice. In the transition, there is a lot of financing support to upgrade skills, manufacturing facilities and testing facilities. That is why a four-year period is used instead of one year. If everything were removed in a single year, things would be different. This is a transition and a facilitation. We know how much employment depends on these industries, so the Government is conscious of it and will implement it carefully over time

Q: What are the budgetary measures to offset the losses incurred by private oil companies this year and in 2027 from buying high and selling low, in order to stabilise livelihoods, given high oil prices and the huge losses suffered by the companies because of the subsidy?

A: Thank you for the question. May I ask one back: is there a cap on the retail price your company is allowed to sell at?

Q: Yes, there is a pricing cap. As per the agreement, the costing formula is not implemented, so we are capped at the price at which CPC sells.

A: I'm sure many understand the predicament the whole world has been through because of the Middle East war. The extent of the oil price increase was so huge that governments across the world had to intervene. Sri Lanka did the same. The Government subsidised a particular component, and it was provided to the SOE and to the private sector, so it is not supporting only the private sector. When the market was opened for competition, the expectation was that there would be suppliers larger than Sri Lanka's own, with a better ability to manage such situations. Sri Lanka is a small market of about 22 million people. CPC serves it at limited capacity, and the rest of the market is shared by other suppliers.

Our approach is to look at it from the point of view of citizens and of the millions of businesses out there. What is best for each? That is why options are identified in consultation and collaboration, and support is given where necessary. Intervening or controlling what businesses can do is the last thing the Government wants to do. We want to give freedom to the most capable and competitive parties to mobilise their capital to supply the needs of Sri Lankan consumers. I know a price limit applies to CPC, and CPC must comply with it. As an SOE, there are limits on subsidising it per se. So whatever relief package has been announced for October, November and December is on a very strict basis and goes down step by step, Rs. 15 billion, then Rs. 13.5 billion, and so on, over a period of three months.  This recognises that subsidising is not the way. But where the need is compelling, the Government cannot turn a blind eye and has to intervene. Thereby the businesses can continue to provide employment, supplies are available, tractors can run at affordable prices, and food security is not at risk. At the larger level there are multiple dimensions to look at, but we are trying to see what facilitation the Government can provide.

That is why I asked about the price. I've noted that some pumps are already at above CPC's price. 

So that's why I said, certain prices are allowed, certain businesses are allowed to consider those prices as well.

Q: The Central Bank's latest progress report noted that the construction and industry sectors have done well, whereas agriculture, I think, shows a negative growth rate. Most of the employment is in agriculture. Is there anything we could do to make it positive within the current quarter?

A: This issue has been recognised. A large amount of land and a large share of the population are engaged in agriculture, yet the contribution to GDP is limited, in the 7% range. Employment in agriculture was about 29% and is now down to about 23%. In land allocation, it is about 39%. So there is definitely an imbalance. It did not happen in one day; it built up over many decades.

That is why this Budget has a specific proposal giving farmers the freedom to decide whether to continue in agriculture and which crop to grow. In the past, farmers were sometimes compelled to grow particular crops because fertiliser subsidies were given only for certain selected crops. This time farmers are free to choose their crop, and the new crop they select will also receive the subsidy. It is a new policy approach to let them cultivate crops that provide higher yields, and so higher family incomes and a higher contribution to GDP. The issue is well recognised and strategies are in place, but it will take a longer period, because about 23% plus of the population is engaged in this area.

But the speculation that there will be challenges in the near future is completely unfounded. I think the President addressed that concern during his Budget speech. In 2025 alone, the amount we paid in foreign-currency debt servicing was more than the amount we are due to pay in 2028. It is a popular tagline for many reasons, but we should recognise that it is unfounded, and also that there are many areas where we can improve implementation

Q: Vehicles came up a number of times when we talked about energy and electricity. Why are you not using fiscal policy to shape the market towards more EVs?

A: The policy signal has already been given. That is why EVs are charged a much lower tax. When we started in 2025, the tax structure was built on the level of pollution. To simplify, diesel combustion has the highest tax, petrol and hybrid versions are in the middle, and EVs have the lowest. That fiscal structure is already being used to accommodate the requirements, though it is based on motor power. It is debatable whether it should be the power of the motor or the power the motor delivers to the wheels. Those are details we can look at. Yes, suggestions are available, and we will continue to improve in those areas. 

Q: What criteria were used to set these priorities and amounts to SMEs, and how will you track whether the funds are actually reaching these groups?

A: The SME sector is built on priorities. That is why women-led businesses, the fisheries sector, young entrepreneurs and the agriculture sector were selected on a prioritised basis for financing, and the amounts allocated are also based on those priorities. A larger amount for a particular sector is also decided on that basis. The Government decides these priorities, and we follow up on whether the prioritised schemes are getting adequate attention in implementation.

The post-Budget Forum’s strategic partner was Standard Chartered Bank; Baurs served as the Gold Sponsor, with Nanaska as Strategic Learning Partner, CICRA as the Technology Partner, Cinnamon Grand as Hospitality Partner and Ogilvy Digital as the Creative Partner.
